procedural_history.originating_court: Independent Mining Local Board, Chhindwara (later Janapada Sabha, Chhindwara)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated May 3, 1966, of the Madhya Pradesh High Court in Misc. Petitions Nos. 552 of 1964 etc.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Madhya Pradesh High Court declared that the Madhya Pradesh Koyala Upkar (Manyatakaran) Adhiniyam (Madhya Pradesh Coal Cess (Validation) Act) 18 of 1964 does not give legal effect to the imposition of cess at the rate of 4 pies, 7 pies and 9 pies per ton under the notifications issued by the Independent Mining Local Board on December 22, 1943, July 29, 1946 and July 19, 1947 respectively, nor to anything done in pursuance of those notifications.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Janapada Sabha, Chhindwara, appealed the High Court's judgment to the Supreme Court because the High Court invalidated the cess imposed by the Independent Mining Local Board (and later collected by the Janapada Sabha) on coal extracted within the area.

directions: The appeals fail and are dismissed with costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Legislature has the power to overrule or set aside a binding judgment of a court by enacting a law that declares the judgment ineffective.

facts: A prior Supreme Court judgment (in The Amalgamated Coalfields Ltd.'s case) had declared a cess invalidly imposed because the required sanction from the State Government had not been obtained.
In response, the Legislature passed a new Act.
This new Act stated that, notwithstanding any court judgment to the contrary, the cess should be deemed to have always been validly imposed.
law: The Court established a clear distinction between permissible and impermissible legislative actions concerning court judgments.
It is permissible for a legislature to amend a law retrospectively, thereby changing the legal basis on which a judgment was made and curing the defect identified by the court.

It is not permissible for a legislature to directly overrule or set aside a binding judgment of a court by simply declaring that the judgment is ineffective. This would be an encroachment on the judicial power.
application: The Court analyzed the new Act and found that it did not actually amend the original law to cure the defect (the lack of government sanction).
Instead, the Act simply declared that the cess was valid, in direct contradiction to the Court's prior ruling.
The Court characterized this as a plain attempt by the Legislature to "overrule or set aside the decision of this Court," rather than to validly change the law retrospectively.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the Legislature's attempt to validate the cess. It concluded that the Legislature cannot simply declare a binding court judgment to be ineffective; it must instead cure the legal defect identified by the court through a retrospective amendment to the underlying law. Since the Legislature failed to do this and instead tried to directly nullify the judgment, its action was unconstitutional.

issue.issue_text: Whether the cess imposed and levied at enhanced rates without the sanction of the State Government was validly imposed.

facts: A local board initially levied a cess on coal at 3 pies per ton, for which it had obtained the required sanction from the Local Government.
The board later enhanced the rate of the cess in 1943, 1946, and 1947, but did so without obtaining the previous sanction of the government for these increases.

The validity of these enhancements was challenged, and the Supreme Court had previously held in 'The Amalgamated Coalfields Ltd.'s' case that the increased levy was illegal because the required government sanction had not been obtained.

In response, the State Legislature enacted a new law, the Madhya Pradesh Koyala Upkar (Manyatakaran) Adhinayam, 1964, which attempted to retroactively validate the cess collected at the enhanced rates, notwithstanding any court judgment.
law: The C.P. Local Self Government Act, 1920, required the previous sanction of the State Government to levy a cess.
The Supreme Court had previously interpreted this to mean that any increase in the rate of the cess also required prior government sanction.
A judgment by the Supreme Court is binding between the parties involved.
Under Article 141 of the Constitution, a declaration of law by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts in India.
A legislature cannot pass a law to simply declare that a court's declaration of law is erroneous, invalid, or ineffective.
application: The Court relied on its previous judgment in 'The Amalgamated Coalfields Ltd.'s' case, which had already established that the cess was not validly imposed at the enhanced rates.
The specific defect identified in the prior case was the failure to obtain the sanction of the State Government before enhancing the rate of the tax.
The Court found that this prior judgment was binding on the parties and, more broadly, as a declaration of law under Article 141.

The Court concluded that the subsequent validating Act passed by the legislature did not give legal effect to the imposition of the cess at the enhanced rates because the legislature could not simply overrule the Court's declaration of law and pronounce it ineffective.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the validity of the cess at the enhanced rates, holding that it was not validly imposed because the mandatory sanction of the State Government was not obtained for the rate increases. The Court affirmed its prior binding judgment on this issue and found that the legislature's subsequent attempt to retroactively validate the cess was ineffective.

issue.issue_text: Whether the validating Act passed by the Legislature gave legal effect to the imposition of cess at the enhanced rates.

facts: A local board initially levied a cess on coal at 3 pies per ton with the required government sanction.
The board later increased the cess rate on three separate occasions (to 4, 7, and 9 pies) without obtaining the necessary government sanction for these enhancements.
In a prior case (The Amalgamated Coalfields Ltd.'s case), the Supreme Court had already ruled that these enhanced levies were illegal and invalid because they lacked the required sanction.

In response to this judgment, the State Legislature passed a validating Act in 1964. This Act stated that, notwithstanding any court judgment, the enhanced cesses were to be considered validly imposed all along, as if the original law had been amended to empower the board to make those enhancements.
law: A judgment of the Supreme Court is binding on the parties involved and, under Article 141 of the Constitution, is the law of the land, binding on all courts.
The legislature has the power to amend a law retrospectively to cure a defect pointed out by a court.

However, the legislature does not have the power to directly overrule a judicial decision or declare that a court's declaration of law is erroneous, invalid, or ineffective. This would be an encroachment on judicial power.
application: The Supreme Court found that the 1964 validating Act was an attempt by the legislature to do what it is not permitted to do: directly overrule a binding judicial decision.
The Court's previous judgment in *The Amalgamated Coalfields Ltd.'s case* had definitively declared the enhanced levy invalid.

Instead of properly curing the defect identified by the court (the lack of sanction), the legislature passed an Act that simply stated the court's declaration of law was ineffective and that the levy was, in fact, valid. The Court viewed this as the legislature impermissibly saying that the Court's prior judgment was wrong.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the validating Act was effective. It held that the Act did not give legal effect to the imposition of cess at the enhanced rates because the legislature cannot simply declare a binding judgment of the Court to be invalid or ineffective.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Legislature has the power to overrule or set aside a binding judgment of a court by enacting a law that declares the judgment ineffective.
appellant_arguments: The Legislature has the power to amend an Act retrospectively and declare what the law shall be deemed to have been, which effectively validates actions previously held invalid by a court.
respondent_arguments: It is not open to the Legislature to say that a judgment of a Court, properly rendered, shall be deemed ineffective. While the legislature can amend laws, it cannot directly overrule a binding judgment or declare that the interpretation of the law shall be otherwise than as declared by the Court, as this is an encroachment on judicial power.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the cess imposed and levied at enhanced rates without the sanction of the State Government was validly imposed.
appellant_arguments: The cess was validly imposed at the enhanced rates.
respondent_arguments: The cess was not validly imposed because the sanction of the State Government was not obtained for enhancing the rate. The expression 'first imposition' in the law includes every increase of the levy, and therefore the increased levy required previous sanction from the government, which was not obtained.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the validating Act passed by the Legislature gave legal effect to the imposition of cess at the enhanced rates.
appellant_arguments: The validating Act, which states that the cess shall be deemed to have always been validly imposed 'as if the enactment... stood amended', successfully gave legal effect to the enhanced cess by retrospectively curing the defect in the law.
respondent_arguments: The validating Act did not give legal effect to the enhanced cess because it was an unconstitutional attempt to declare a binding judgment ineffective, rather than genuinely curing the legal defect identified by the court.

cases.case_name: The Amalgamated Coalfields Ltd. v. Janapada Sabha, Chhindwara
cases.principle: It is not open to the Legislature to say that a judgment of a Court properly constituted and rendered in exercise of its power shall be deemed to be ineffective and the interpretation of the law shall be otherwise than as declared by the Court.

cases.case_name: Cape Brandy Syndicate v. Commissioners of Inland Revenue
cases.principle: If an Act does not by the plain language used therein carry out its object, the Court will not be justified in supplying deficiencies in the Act, especially in a taxing statute.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: While the Legislature may retrospectively amend a law to alter the basis of a judicial decision, it is not open to the Legislature to directly declare that a judgment of a court is ineffective or that the interpretation of the law shall be otherwise than as declared by the court.
obiter: In a taxing Act, one must look merely at what is clearly said, as there is no room for intendment, equity, or presumption. Nothing is to be read in or implied; one can only look fairly at the language used.
If an Act does not carry out its object by its plain language, the Court is not justified in supplying deficiencies in the Act.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: On the words used in the Act, it is plain that the Legislature attempted to overrule or set aside the decision of this Court. It is not open to the Legislature to say that a judgment of a Court properly constituted and rendered in exercise of its power in a matter brought before it shall be deemed to be ineffective and the interpretation of the law shall be otherwise than as declared by the Court.
legal_tests_applied: It is open to the Legislature within certain limits to amend the provisions of an Act retrospectively and to declare what the law shall be deemed to have been, but it is not open to the Legislature to say that a judgment of a Court properly constituted and rendered shall be deemed to be ineffective.

In a taxing Act one has to look merely at what is clearly said. There is no room for any intendment: There is no equity about a tax. There is no presumption as to a tax. Nothing is to be read in, nothing is to be implied. One can only look fairly at the language used.
why_appellant_lost: The validating Act was an unconstitutional attempt by the Legislature to overrule or set aside a binding decision of the court, which is an impermissible encroachment on judicial power.

The validating Act failed to actually cure the legal defect identified by the court. The Act did not amend the underlying law to retroactively provide for the missing government sanction; it merely declared the court's judgment ineffective.

The prior judgment holding that the cess was not validly imposed because the sanction of the State Government was not obtained was binding between the parties and, by virtue of Article 141, on all courts in India.
why_respondent_won: The Legislature cannot say that a judgment of a court properly rendered shall be deemed to be ineffective either as a precedent or between the parties.
The prior judgment of the Court, which held that the cess was not validly imposed due to the lack of sanction from the State Government, was binding and could not be legislatively nullified.

The validating Act did not give legal effect to the imposition of cess because it did not actually amend the law to cure the defect, but instead impermissibly attempted to set aside the court's decision.
policy_considerations: Under our constitutional scheme, it is not open to the Legislature to overrule or set aside a binding judgment of a court, as this would violate the separation of powers.
